classes_note: Three classes, each the census's own intersection, evidence kind or finding for the entity, stated by field sources at the loci given: (1) the dating of the New Testament writings (census intersection 'nt-scholarship', evidence_kind 'dating table'; B1, B2); (2) the late (Domitianic) date of Revelation and its Irenaean anchor (census findings[1], evidence rev_range and rev_domitian; B2, the Revelation page and its quoted Kümmel introduction); (3) the Pauline letters as the earliest New Testament writings (census findings[0], does_not_answer[1]; B1, the dating table). The archive bears on these classes through the Revelation First thesis (#202, its claim ladder and falsifiers, and the deposits revelationfirst.com cites); a deposit enters only where its sentence says something of the entity or applies its category (the Domitianic consensus as an inferential settlement, Pauline priority as inferential, the received chronology, Revelation First) to one of these classes. The census's rf_intersection ('Dating, as the received order: Paul at 50-60 and Revelation at 90-95, the late date and the order Revelation First contests, laid out as a table') and its correction are the archive's reading, ledgered as RF-; they do not by themselves admit a deposit. Not classes: the census's kind 'an online collection of early Christian texts' (no field source sets the entity in a class the archive applies a category to; the archive's originals library seats texts in the original language and is a different object), and 'the Apostolic Fathers' (a category of B1's menu and the homonym's contents; no census field names it for the entity). Aliases: the name as a proper name, case-sensitive (lower-case 'early Christian writings' is the generic phrase, read as such), the site's host, and its operator as the site names him. Archive uses of the Penguin book's title are read as the homonym's and recorded, never admitted as the entity's. Admission by reading (§3.4): a bare mention, a reference-list entry or a keyword is not a claim.
